title: If AI makes game creation ridiculously easy, what becomes the next big bottleneck in game development?
author: SouthernSinger5456
selftext:
I've been thinking about where game development goes as AI game-building tools get significantly better.

Platforms like CodeWisp, Playabl and other AI game builders are pushing toward a world where creating a playable game becomes much faster and accessible to almost anyone.

But if **creation itself becomes cheap and abundant**, what becomes difficult?

Is the next big problem:

* getting people to discover your game?
* finding the right playtesters?
* turning prototypes into genuinely good games?
* retention/community?
* monetization?
* standing out when thousands more games are being released?
* something completely different?

I'm especially curious to hear from indie/solo developers: **what part of game development do you think AI won't solve just by making creation easier?**

comments.author: tabaxi_gf

Games take a lot of iteration to try things; not just in prototypes because usually new mechanics and levels are added later after the initial prototype is agreed on. The bottleneck is humans testing and feeling through these changes to confirm they are fun or worthwhile.   
When AI can figure that out, it will be able to complete the loop and generate an entire fun, interesting game. Don’t see that happening for some time though even with the rate we’re going since fun, feel and interest are such nebulous human concepts.

replies.author: Little_Beyond_9163

Getting AI to truly operate on human brain levels of abstraction is a task we genuinely have no idea how close we are to completing.

Current frontier model development isn’t even heading that direction right now. Its more like “how much more efficiently can I expand this prediction system to predict better and faster” instead of “how can I get a computer to look at things the way a human would”.

This is the chasm between LLMs and human creativity.

Yes, creation is easy, scaling, business and growth is much harder. We're having a conferenc eon this exact topic:

* [Rapid Prototyping](https://www.glitch.fun/gameshows/9eadde86-a1b2-4882-86e4-a3e9e2e08814/schedule/01a04a3f-bcfc-7127-8523-8b7e9bf53b74/standalone)

The gist is. this whats important is first finding "product/market" fit, which means that people actually want to your game. Can you learn how to position your game, explain,make it sound exciting? You can do that with rough protortpes and trailers.

One you do that, can you create a core loop people like. How long do  people play your game?

After you nail those then, then you focus on user acquistion. This is all part of building the game, not after after you build the game.

comments.author: zayelion

A game consist of game mechanics, visual art, sound design, music, narration/writing, UI/UX expertise, and a host of other minor skills. AI accellerates them all but its not mastery. "Make a good game" is still the big bottle neck of any random idea becoming a profitable/famous game. AI really 1 shots game mechanics, and its slowly moving into assets. It hasnt mastered them. Also the mechancis take a while to get down too. About a weeks worth of tokens to get mechanics down if the game has decent complexity and more than 1 game loop.

After that, its marketing, you basically still need to throw money or large amounts of time and skill at the problem. Right now I burn more tokens on marketing 1 game than I do on development of 4 different ones. Its even more hyper saturated and money is the number 1 solution still.

comments.author: Meatgortex
comments.body:
The web came with the promise that everyone could be a published author. Why didn’t that happen? Because most people don’t have the skills to write something that others find interesting. 

AI will make parts of full game development (not just prototypes or small games) faster. But that doesn’t mean that it will make more people that can create interesting games. We will see a massive amount of copycat titles that mimic quality games but without bringing anything new to the table or understanding the subtleties that make the original work. 

Some of these may be commercially viable, but players will quickly adapt to being able to distinguish between titles with cohesive and intrinsic value and those that are weak mimics.

comments.author: LocoMod
comments.body:
In the end it all comes down to one thing: fun

You can make a very simple game, with simple graphics, and if its fun people will value it. Simple as that.

This is a subjective value judgement and that means AI won't solve it, ever, precisely because it's not a "provable" thing. People have different views on what they consider fun. And there is no single recipe for that.

So it doesn't matter how graphically impressive or complex the game is. If it's not fun, then its just a tech demo as far as the audience is concerned. Sometimes this has value in and of itself. But it needs to be REALLY impressive for people to value that. And even then, a portion of them won't. And that's fine. 

That's just how it goes.

comments.body: Biggest bottle neck will be 3d modeling. Tripo and meshy are good but way too expensive. Fable and astra both can create models that are okay for a play test but are no where near ready for a releasable game. Ive noticed that AI, even tho its capable of generating nice ui's especially with open ais image model, it tends to suck at actually doing ui's. After 3d modeling gets solved (either tripo or meshy stop charging out the wazoo per model, or models can create production ready models on their own) the bottle neck will be gameplay/story. Models also struggle heavily with creating a cohesive story or something that draws you in. Tbh I think that should be left to humans either way tho. comments.author: Standard_Rabbit706
comments.body: The bottleneck is still taste. It will always be taste. They could invent a machine that is literally one button, it reads your mind, and it makes a game that is as good on a technical level as any AAA game, and most games would suck. Because people don’t have taste. And taste is not something you’re born with. Taste is something you developed. And you developed it by DOING WORK. By messing up and learning and trying again. Which is something that you don’t get with AI. And the “better” AI gets, the fewer people will go through that process and the worse games will get. The best games will continue to be made by the few who put in the work over a long time.

comments.author: SilliCarl
comments.body:
I think that in 10 years individual games wont be around. Instead everyone will have an AI and they will describe the game they want to play to the AI, it will then develop that game and build it on your PC, custom just for you - in a similar time to what it would take to download a large game. Then you'll play the game for however long, delete it and then have it build a new game for you. 

Maybe 10 years is too close, but eventually I think this will be the way things go.
